# Overview

This is the **code-along** version of Example 2. In the workshop, Example 1
(the face-emotion study) walked through every line of code with you. This time
**you're in the driver's seat**: we give you the data, the research question,
and hints, and you write the code and make the modeling decisions.

We'll model the mismatch negativity (MMN) from an **auditory oddball**
(participants hear a frequent **standard** sound and a rare **deviant** sound)
**trial by trial**: each deviant is paired with the standard right before it,
and the outcome is their difference, a **single-trial MMN difference wave** (as
in Mon et al., 2024).

The full worked version is `LME_ex2_oddball.Rmd`, and a supplement
(`LME_ex2_supplement_interaction.Rmd`) fits the same data as a Condition × Age
interaction instead of a difference wave.

## How to use this code-along

- **"Your turn" chunks** are mostly empty. Each one comes with a task and
  hints (which functions to use, what to check). Write the code yourself;
  Example 1 and the slides are fair game to copy from.
- **"Solution / catch up" chunks** come right after each "Your turn". Their
  code is folded: click **Code** to see it. **Run each one either way:** if your
  code worked, it just recreates the same objects (with the names the next
  steps use); if you got stuck, fell behind, or got an error, it fills in the
  step for you.
- **"Show answer" boxes** hold our answers to the questions (and our
  modeling decisions). Decide for yourself first, then click to compare.
  There's often more than one defensible answer.
- **Lost completely?** Click on the next chunk and use **Run All Chunks Above**
  (the ▼ button at the top right of the chunk, or Ctrl+Alt+P / Cmd+Option+P).
  That runs everything before it, including the solution chunks, so you can
  pick up at any step.

# Simulating an Oddball Study

## Study design

*Read this section and run the chunks as they are: you don't need to change anything until the descriptive statistics.*

**Our simulation** is loosely based on oddball designs like those in Mon et
al. (2024) and Coy et al. (2024):

- **Participants:** 40, aged 2 to 4 years
- **Stimuli:** a standard syllable /ba/ and a deviant /da/, with the deviant
  recorded by 6 speakers (6 **recordings/speakers**, or "tokens")
- **Trials:** 600 standards and 150 deviants (25 per token) per participant
- **Outcome:** a single-trial MMN for every deviant: the deviant minus the
  standard right before it

The population values for the MMN come from Coy et al. (2024, Table 1):

- Standard: ~**1.9 µV**; deviant: ~**0 µV**, so the MMN is ~**−1.9 µV**
- SD of the MMN across participants: 0.148 × √60 ≈ **1.15 µV**
- SD of the standard amplitude across participants: 0.187 × √60 ≈ **1.45 µV**

The additional parameters (habituation, the token and age effects, and the
single-trial noise) are our own choices.

```{r design-params}
# Study design parameters --------------------------------------------------
n_subjects     <- 40     # number of participants
n_tokens       <- 6      # recordings/speakers of the deviant /da/
dev_per_token  <- 25     # deviants per token per participant
n_deviant      <- n_tokens * dev_per_token   # 150 deviants per participant
n_standard     <- 4 * n_deviant              # 600 standards per participant (80% of trials)

# Population-level parameters (MMN size and variability from Coy et al., 2024) --
mean_amp_standard <- 1.9    # mean amplitude for standards (µV)
mmn_effect        <- -1.9   # MMN (deviant - standard) at the middle of the session (µV)
subject_int_sd    <- 1.45   # SD of participants' standard amplitude
subject_mmn_sd    <- 1.15   # SD of participants' MMN (random intercept in the MMN model)
int_mmn_cor       <- -0.3   # correlation between participants' standard amplitude and MMN

# Additional parameters ---------------------------------------------------------
hab_effect        <- 0.15   # MMN becomes less negative by this much per 10 deviants (habituation)
subject_hab_sd    <- 0.2    # participants habituate at different rates (SD per 10 deviants)
age_effect        <- -0.5   # MMN becomes more negative by this much per year of age
token_sd          <- 0.5    # some /da/ recordings/speakers elicit a larger MMN than others
trial_noise_sd    <- 7      # single-trial noise SD (each trial, standard or deviant)

set.seed(2026)
```

## Building the trial-level dataset

Each simulated participant hears a sequence in which every deviant follows at
least two standards (so every deviant has a standard right before it, as in
typical oddball designs). Each simulated participant gets their own standard
amplitude, MMN size, and habituation rate, and each /da/ token has its own MMN
shift.

```{r simulate-data}
subject_ids <- sprintf("%02d", 1:n_subjects)

# Participant-level random effects: correlated standard amplitude + MMN, habituation rate, age
re_cov <- matrix(c(subject_int_sd^2,
                   int_mmn_cor * subject_int_sd * subject_mmn_sd,
                   int_mmn_cor * subject_int_sd * subject_mmn_sd,
                   subject_mmn_sd^2), nrow = 2)
subject_re <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_subjects, mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = re_cov) %>%
  as_tibble(.name_repair = ~ c("subj_intercept", "subj_mmn")) %>%
  mutate(SubjectID = subject_ids,
         subj_hab  = rnorm(n_subjects, 0, subject_hab_sd),
         AgeYears  = round(runif(n_subjects, 2, 4), 1))

# Token-level random effects
token_re <- tibble(Token = paste0("da", 1:n_tokens),
                   token_mmn = rnorm(n_tokens, 0, token_sd))

# One participant's sequence: each deviant follows at least 2 standards; the remaining
# standards are spread at random, and the 6 tokens appear in random order
make_sequence <- function() {
  extra <- as.vector(rmultinom(1, n_standard - 2 * n_deviant, rep(1, n_deviant)))
  tokens <- sample(rep(paste0("da", 1:n_tokens), dev_per_token))
  map2_dfr(2 + extra, seq_len(n_deviant), function(k, i)
    tibble(Condition = c(rep("Standard", k), "Deviant"),
           Token     = c(rep(NA, k), tokens[i])))
}

oddball_data <- map_dfr(subject_ids, ~ make_sequence() %>% mutate(SubjectID = .x)) %>%
  group_by(SubjectID) %>%
  mutate(TrialNum = row_number(),
         DevNum   = if_else(Condition == "Deviant", cumsum(Condition == "Deviant"), NA_integer_)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  left_join(subject_re, by = "SubjectID") %>%
  left_join(token_re, by = "Token") %>%
  mutate(
    # the MMN on this deviant: average MMN + participant + habituation + age + token
    mmn = if_else(Condition == "Deviant",
                  mmn_effect + subj_mmn +
                    (hab_effect + subj_hab) * (DevNum - mean(1:n_deviant)) / 10 +
                    age_effect * (AgeYears - 3) + token_mmn,
                  0),
    MeanAmp   = mean_amp_standard + subj_intercept + mmn + rnorm(n(), 0, trial_noise_sd),
    Condition = factor(Condition, levels = c("Standard", "Deviant"))
  ) %>%
  select(SubjectID, AgeYears, TrialNum, Condition, Token, DevNum, MeanAmp)

glimpse(oddball_data)
```

## Single-trial difference waves

We pair each deviant with the **standard immediately before it** and subtract:
MMN = deviant − preceding standard. Each pair is one row in the analysis
dataset. We also keep the standard and deviant amplitudes themselves, so that
the same pairs can be modeled as a Condition × Age **interaction**
instead of a difference wave (see the supplement, `LME_ex2_supplement_interaction.Rmd`).

```{r difference-waves}
mmn_data <- oddball_data %>%
  group_by(SubjectID) %>%
  mutate(prev_condition = lag(Condition),
         prev_amp       = lag(MeanAmp)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(Condition == "Deviant", prev_condition == "Standard") %>%
  transmute(SubjectID, AgeYears, Token, DevNum,
            Standard = prev_amp,            # the standard right before the deviant
            Deviant  = MeanAmp,             # the deviant
            MMN      = Deviant - Standard)  # single-trial difference wave

glimpse(mmn_data)

# Pairs per participant (every deviant here has a standard right before it)
mmn_data %>% count(SubjectID) %>% summarise(min = min(n), max = max(n))
```

A few things to notice:

- **Only the standards right before a deviant are used** (150 of each
  participant's 600). In real data, a pair is lost whenever *either* trial is
  rejected, so you can lose more data than with averaging (Mon et al., 2024). In our simulation, we won't simulate any missing data.
- **Difference waves have more noise than amplitude in a single condition.** Each pair contains the noise from two trials, so the
  single-trial noise SD of the MMN is about √2 × `r trial_noise_sd` ≈
  `r round(sqrt(2) * trial_noise_sd, 1)` µV.

# Descriptive Statistics & Data Visualization

**Your turn:** before modeling, look at the data. Make (at least) these plots
with `mmn_data`:

1. The distribution of the single-trial MMNs (`geom_histogram()`).
2. Each participant's MMN across the session. Single trials are very noisy, so
   average them in blocks first (e.g., `Block = ceiling(DevNum / 25)`, then
   `group_by(SubjectID, Block)` and `summarise()`), and draw one line per
   participant (`aes(group = SubjectID)`).
3. Each participant's mean MMN for each `/da/` token.

What do you notice? Is there an MMN on average? Does it change over the
session? Do the tokens differ?

```{r data-plotting-solution, class.source = "fold-hide"}
# Distribution of single-trial MMNs
ggplot(mmn_data, aes(x = MMN)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Single-trial MMN: deviant − preceding standard (µV)", y = "Count",
       title = "Single-trial MMN difference waves")

# Each participant's MMN across the session (averaged in blocks of 25 deviants)
mmn_data %>%
  mutate(Block = ceiling(DevNum / 25)) %>%
  group_by(SubjectID, Block) %>%
  summarise(MMN = mean(MMN), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Block, y = MMN, group = SubjectID)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.25) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1.5, color = "#D55E00") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6, labels = paste0(seq(1, 126, 25), "–", seq(25, 150, 25))) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Deviants", y = "Mean MMN (µV)",
       title = "MMN across the session (orange = average)")

# MMN for each /da/ token: each participant's mean MMN for that token
mmn_data %>%
  group_by(SubjectID, Token) %>%
  summarise(MMN = mean(MMN), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Token, y = MMN)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_violin(fill = "#3D6080", alpha = 0.25, color = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3.5, color = "#D55E00") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "/da/ token (recording/speaker)", y = "Participant's mean MMN (µV)",
       title = "MMN for each /da/ recording/speaker",
       subtitle = "Violins and gray points = participants' means; orange = token mean")

# Each participant's mean MMN across tokens
ggplot(aes(x = SubjectID, y = MMN, color = Token), data = mmn_data) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.25, alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 2, color = "pink") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Subject ID", y = "Participant's mean MMN (µV)",
       title = "Distribution of single-trial MMNs for each participant")
```

# Fitting an LME: the 9 steps

## Step 1: Define the research question

**Your turn:** write the research question in one sentence. (Hint: look at the
study design. Which participant-level variable did we vary?)

<details>
<summary>Show answer</summary>

Does the MMN change with age?

</details>

## Step 2: List all relevant variables

**Your turn:** list the variables you'll need from `mmn_data` (run
`glimpse(mmn_data)`). Which is the outcome?

```{r list-variables-yourturn}

```

<details>
<summary>Show answer</summary>

- `MMN`: single-trial difference wave (deviant − preceding standard), the outcome
- `AgeYears`: participant's age
- `DevNum`: presentation number of the deviant (1st, 2nd, … 150th)
- `SubjectID`: participant
- `Token`: which /da/ recording/speaker was played

</details>

## Step 3: Draw the study design schematic

**Your turn:** sketch the design on paper first. Which grouping factors are
there? Are they crossed or nested? Then run the chunk below to compare.

```{r design-diagram-solution, fig.height=5.5, class.source = "fold-hide"}
subj_nodes  <- tibble(label = c("Subject 01", "Subject 02", "Subject 03", "…",
                                paste("Subject", n_subjects)),
                      x = 1:5, y = 2)
token_nodes <- tibble(label = paste0("/da/ ", 1:n_tokens),
                      x = seq(0.8, 5.2, length.out = n_tokens), y = 1)
pair_nodes  <- token_nodes %>% mutate(y = 0, label = "std → dev")
edges <- expand_grid(x = subj_nodes$x[subj_nodes$label != "…"],
                     xend = token_nodes$x)

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = 2, yend = 1), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_segment(data = token_nodes, aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 1, yend = 0), colour = "grey45") +
  geom_label(data = filter(subj_nodes, label != "…"), aes(x, y, label = label),
             fill = "#9CAF88", colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(data = filter(subj_nodes, label == "…"), aes(x, y, label = label), size = 6) +
  geom_label(data = token_nodes, aes(x, y, label = label),
             fill = "#3D6080", colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_label(data = pair_nodes, aes(x, y, label = label),
             fill = "#D55E00", colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3) +
  annotate("label", x = 3, y = 1.5, fill = "white", size = 3.5,
           label = "every subject hears every /da/ token") +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = -0.38, size = 3.5, fontface = "italic",
           label = paste0("each token: ", dev_per_token,
                          " deviants per subject, \neach paired with the standard before it  →  ",
                          n_subjects, " × ", n_tokens, " × ", dev_per_token, " = ",
                          n_subjects * n_deviant, " single-trial MMNs")) +
  labs(title = "Subjects and tokens are crossed") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.3)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```

## Step 4: Categorize variables by type & level (trial vs. subject)

**Your turn:** for each variable from Step 2, is it continuous or categorical?
Does it vary from trial to trial, or only between participants? Which ones are
grouping factors?

<details>
<summary>Show answer</summary>

- `MMN`: continuous, trial-level (outcome)
- `AgeYears`: continuous, participant-level
- `DevNum`: continuous, trial-level
- `Token`: categorical, trial-level (grouping factor: a sample of possible recordings/speakers)
- `SubjectID`: categorical, participant-level (grouping factor)

</details>

## Step 5: Assign fixed and random effects

**Your turn:**

1. Which **fixed effects** do you need? One answers the research question;
   is there a covariate that could matter in a long oddball session?
2. For each grouping factor, list the **possible random effects**, and write
   each as a question ("Do participants differ in …?"). Hint: a random slope
   only makes sense if the predictor varies *within* that grouping factor.
   Can participants differ in their age effect?
3. Write the **maximal model** as an `lmer()` formula. Is there more than one
   reasonable maximal model, depending on your hypothesis?

<details>
<summary>Show answer</summary>

**Fixed effects**

- Age (our research question)
- Presentation number (a covariate: the MMN may habituate over the session)

**Possible random effects in our design**

*SubjectID*

- `(1 | SubjectID)`: Do participants differ in the size of their MMN?
- `(1 + DevNum | SubjectID)`: Do participants habituate at different rates?

*Token*

- `(1 | Token)`: Do some /da/ recordings/speakers elicit a larger MMN than others?
- `(1 + DevNum | Token)`: Does the MMN habituate faster for some recordings/speakers?
- `(1 + Age | Token)`: Does the age effect differ across recordings/speakers?

There is no `(1 + Age | SubjectID)`: each participant has only one age, so
participants can't differ in an age effect.

**Two possible maximal models**

The maximal model depends on your hypothesis. Either of these is reasonable:

**A. Habituation is the same at every age.** Presentation number and age are
separate fixed effects:

```
MMN ~ DevNum_gmc + Age_gmc +
      (1 + DevNum_gmc | SubjectID) +
      (1 + DevNum_gmc + Age_gmc | Token)
```

**B. The habituation rate changes with age.** If you expected older children's
MMNs to fade faster (or slower) over the session, you would add the
**DevNum × Age interaction**. Random slopes only include terms that are in the
fixed effects, so the by-token slopes get the interaction too (tokens could
differ in how much age changes habituation). Participants still get only a
habituation slope, because each has one age:

```
MMN ~ DevNum_gmc * Age_gmc +
      (1 + DevNum_gmc | SubjectID) +
      (1 + DevNum_gmc * Age_gmc | Token)
```

Our research question is about the age effect on the MMN, not whether
habituation changes with age, so **we fit Model A**. With Model B, the by-token
interaction slope would be the first thing to remove in Step 7: it's the least
plausible, and with only six tokens it can't be estimated.

</details>

## Step 6: Consider data transformations & center predictors

**Your turn:** add two new columns to `mmn_data`:

- `DevNum_gmc`: presentation number, **grand-mean centered** and expressed in
  **units of 10 deviants** (divide by 10). Why rescale? `DevNum` runs from 1 to
  150, so a slope per single deviant is tiny, and tiny variance components make
  the model hard to estimate.
- `Age_gmc`: age, grand-mean centered. Careful: each participant has 150 rows,
  so compute the mean age from **one row per participant** (`distinct()`), and
  keep it as `age_grandmean` (we use it again to plot).

What will the intercept mean after centering?

```{r center-predictors-yourturn}

```

**Solution / catch up:** run this chunk either way (click **Code** to see it).

```{r center-predictors-solution, class.source = "fold-hide"}
age_grandmean <- mean(distinct(mmn_data, SubjectID, AgeYears)$AgeYears)   # one value per participant

mmn_data <- mmn_data %>%
  mutate(DevNum_gmc = (DevNum - mean(DevNum)) / 10,   # grand-mean centered, in units of 10 deviants
         Age_gmc    = AgeYears - age_grandmean)         # grand-mean centered age

mmn_data %>% select(SubjectID, Token, DevNum, DevNum_gmc, AgeYears, Age_gmc, MMN) %>% head()
```

<details>
<summary>Show answer</summary>

The intercept is the MMN **in the middle of the session for a participant of average age**. 
</details>

## Step 7: Fit the maximal model and simplify until convergence is reached

Run this helper (the same one as in Example 1). It prints whether a fit is
singular and the random-effect SDs and correlations:

```{r check-fit-helper}
check_fit <- function(fit) {
  cat("Singular fit:", isSingular(fit), "\n\n")
  print(VarCorr(fit), comp = "Std.Dev.")  # random-effect SDs and correlations
}
```

### Step 7a: Fit the maximal model

**Your turn:** fill in the random slopes for participants and for tokens
(Model A from Step 5), then run the chunk.

```{r maximal-model-yourturn}
# fit_max <- lmer(MMN...)
```

**Solution / catch up:** run this chunk either way (click **Code** to see it).

```{r maximal-model-solution, warning=TRUE, class.source = "fold-hide"}
fit_max <- lmer(MMN ~ DevNum_gmc + Age_gmc +
                  (1 + DevNum_gmc | SubjectID) +          # participants differ in MMN size and habituation
                  (1 + DevNum_gmc + Age_gmc | Token),     # tokens differ in MMN size, habituation, age effect
                data = mmn_data)

check_fit(fit_max)
```

<details>
<summary>What do the variance components tell us?</summary>

- **Token:** the slope SDs are small and the correlations are at ±1. With only
  `r n_tokens` tokens, there isn't enough information to estimate how tokens
  differ in habituation or age effects.
- **SubjectID:** the habituation slope SD isn't near 0, and the correlation
  isn't at ±1.

</details>

### Steps 7b–7d: Simplifying the model 

```{r model-simplification}

```


<details>
<summary>Show the simplification path</summary>

**Round 1: the by-token age slope** (starting from the maximal model, Step 7a)

- Remove the by-token age slope:
  `(1 + DevNum_gmc | SubjectID) + (1 + DevNum_gmc | Token)`
  → still singular: the by-token habituation slope is tiny and correlated −1
  with the token intercept.

**Round 2: the habituation slopes**

- Remove the by-token habituation slope:
  `(1 + DevNum_gmc | SubjectID) + (1 | Token)`
  → not singular. lme4 gives a borderline convergence warning, which turns out to be a false alarm (see below): **this is our final random-effects
  structure**, so we stop here.
- *If that hadn't worked*, we would put it back and remove the by-participant
  habituation slope instead:
  `(1 | SubjectID) + (1 + DevNum_gmc | Token)`
  → this one is singular (the by-token slope is again correlated −1 with the
  intercept), so it wouldn't have been an option anyway.
- *And if neither had worked*, we would remove both:
  `(1 | SubjectID) + (1 | Token)` (random intercepts only).

</details>


**Solution / catch up:** run this chunk either way (click **Code** to see it).

```{r final-model-solution, warning=TRUE, class.source = "fold-hide"}
fit_final <- lmer(MMN ~ DevNum_gmc + Age_gmc +
                    (1 + DevNum_gmc | SubjectID) +
                    (1 | Token),
                    data = mmn_data,
                    control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

check_fit(fit_final)
performance::check_convergence(fit_final)

```

**Your turn:** write two or three sentences for your methods section
describing how you simplified the model.

<details>
<summary>Show our version</summary>

*"We began with the maximal random-effects structure (Barr et al., 2013) and
simplified it one term at a time until the model converged without a singular
fit, starting with the by-token random slopes (only six tokens): first the
by-token slope of age, then the by-token slope of presentation number. The
final model, fit with the bobyqa optimizer, included by-participant random
intercepts and random slopes of presentation number, a by-token random
intercept, and fixed effects of presentation number (grand-mean centered, in
units of 10 deviants) and age (grand-mean centered)."*

</details>

## Step 8: Check model assumptions

**Your turn:** check the model's assumptions with `check_model()` With this many 
trials, should you use formal tests or visual inspection? 

```{r check-model-yourturn, fig.width=10, fig.height=12}

```

**Solution / catch up:** run this chunk either way (click **Code** to see it).

```{r check-model-solution, fig.width=10, fig.height=12, class.source = "fold-hide"}
check_model(fit_final)  
```

<details>
<summary>Show answer</summary>

With `r format(nobs(fit_final), big.mark = ",")` single-trial MMNs, formal tests (e.g., Shapiro-Wilk for normality or a test for heteroscedasticity) can be significant even when there are only small deviations from the assumption. Some researchers recommend Shapiro-Wilk for samples up to 5,000 but other researchers suggest that Shapiro-Wilk is too sensitive even lower (e.g., at 4,000 observations). Beyond 4,000-5,000 observations/total trials you should use visual inspection: flat reference lines (linearity, homogeneity of variance), dots along the line (normality of residuals and random effects), and points inside the contour lines (influential observations).

</details>

```{r final-output-solution, class.source = "fold-hide"}
b        <- fixef(fit_final)
vc_subj  <- VarCorr(fit_final)$SubjectID
sd_mmn   <- attr(vc_subj, "stddev")[["(Intercept)"]]
sd_hab   <- attr(vc_subj, "stddev")[["DevNum_gmc"]]
cor_mh   <- attr(vc_subj, "correlation")[1, 2]
sd_token <- attr(VarCorr(fit_final)$Token, "stddev")[["(Intercept)"]]
sd_resid <- sigma(fit_final)
coefs    <- summary(fit_final)$coefficients
```

<details>
<summary>Show answer</summary>

**Fixed effects**

- **Age_gmc = `r round(b[["Age_gmc"]], 2)` µV:** the change in the MMN per year
  of age (simulated: `r age_effect` µV; p = `r round(coefs["Age_gmc", "Pr(>|t|)"], 2)`).
  This answers our research question: there's no evidence that the MMN changes
  with age here. Age is a participant-level predictor tested against only
  `r n_subjects` participants (df ≈ `r round(coefs["Age_gmc", "df"])`), so a
  modest age effect is hard to detect.
- **(Intercept) = `r round(b[["(Intercept)"]], 2)` µV:** the MMN in the middle of the
  session for a participant of average age (simulated: `r mmn_effect` µV). Look at
  its df (≈ `r round(coefs["(Intercept)", "df"])`): the average MMN has to
  generalize across participants *and* across the `r n_tokens` tokens, so with
  few tokens, its df is small (like the actors in Example 1).
- **DevNum_gmc = `r round(b[["DevNum_gmc"]], 2)` µV:** the MMN becomes
  `r round(b[["DevNum_gmc"]], 2)` µV less negative with every 10 deviants
  (simulated: `r hab_effect`), so it weakens over the session (habituation).
  Over all `r n_deviant` deviants, that's about
  `r round(b[["DevNum_gmc"]] * n_deviant / 10, 1)` µV. Its df is about
  `r round(coefs["DevNum_gmc", "df"])`: with a random slope, habituation is
  tested against how much participants differ in it.

**Random effects**

- **Participants' MMN, SD = `r round(sd_mmn, 2)` µV** (simulated: `r subject_mmn_sd`):
  participants' MMNs typically differ from the average by about
  `r round(sd_mmn, 1)` µV. About `r round(100 * pnorm(0, mean = b[["(Intercept)"]], sd = sd_mmn))`%
  of participants are expected to show an MMN (a negative difference) in the
  middle of the session.
- **Participants' habituation, SD = `r round(sd_hab, 2)` µV per 10 deviants**
  (simulated: `r subject_hab_sd`): some participants' MMNs fade quickly; others
  barely change.
- **Correlation = `r round(cor_mh, 2)`:** between participants' MMN and their
  habituation (we simulated 0). With `r n_subjects` participants, this is
  estimated imprecisely.
- **Tokens, SD = `r round(sd_token, 2)` µV** (simulated: `r token_sd`): some /da/
  recordings/speakers elicit a larger MMN than others.
- **Residual SD = `r round(sd_resid, 2)` µV:** single-trial noise in the difference
  wave (about √2 × `r trial_noise_sd` = `r round(sqrt(2) * trial_noise_sd, 1)` µV,
  because each MMN contains the noise from two trials).

</details>

### Visualizing the results

1. **The research question: the MMN across age.** Plot the model's estimated
   marginal means across the observed age range, with each participant's mean
   MMN as points. Hints: `emmeans(fit_final, ~ Age_gmc, at = list(Age_gmc =
   age_grid), lmer.df = "asymptotic")`, where `age_grid` is a sequence of
   centered ages; convert back to years with `+ age_grandmean`; use
   `geom_ribbon()` for ± 1 SE.
2. **Habituation, with each participant's line** (the random slope): 
   `coef(fit_final)$SubjectID` gives each participant's own intercept and
   slope.
3. **Caterpillar plot:** a caterpillar plot of each participant's habituation slope
   with a 95% interval. Hint: `as.data.frame(ranef(fit_final, condVar =
   TRUE))` gives each random effect (`condval`) and its SD (`condsd`); add the
   fixed effect back to get each participant's own slope.

**Solution / catch up:** run this chunk either way (click **Code** to see it).

```{r visualize-age-solution, class.source = "fold-hide"}
# Model-estimated MMN across the observed age range (middle of the session), ± 1 SE
age_grid <- seq(min(mmn_data$Age_gmc), max(mmn_data$Age_gmc), length.out = 25)
emm_age <- emmeans(fit_final, ~ Age_gmc, at = list(Age_gmc = age_grid),
                   lmer.df = "asymptotic")

subject_age_means <- mmn_data %>%
  group_by(SubjectID, AgeYears) %>%
  summarise(MMN = mean(MMN), .groups = "drop")

as.data.frame(emm_age) %>%
  mutate(AgeYears = Age_gmc + age_grandmean) %>%          # back to years for the x-axis
  ggplot(aes(x = AgeYears, y = emmean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = subject_age_means, aes(y = MMN), color = "grey55", size = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = emmean - SE, ymax = emmean + SE), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1.3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "MMN (µV)",
       title = "The MMN across age",
       subtitle = "Blue = EMM ± 1 SE (middle of the session); gray = each participant's mean MMN")
```

```{r visualize-habituation-solution, class.source = "fold-hide"}
# Model-estimated MMN across the session (for a participant of average age), ± 1 SE
dev_grid <- seq(min(mmn_data$DevNum_gmc), max(mmn_data$DevNum_gmc), length.out = 30)
emm_dev <- emmeans(fit_final, ~ DevNum_gmc, at = list(DevNum_gmc = dev_grid),
                   lmer.df = "asymptotic")

# Each participant's model-estimated line (fixed effects + their random intercept and slope)
subject_lines <- coef(fit_final)$SubjectID %>%
  rownames_to_column("SubjectID") %>%
  transmute(SubjectID, intercept = `(Intercept)`, slope = DevNum_gmc) %>%
  crossing(x = range(mmn_data$DevNum_gmc)) %>%
  mutate(MMN = intercept + slope * x)

back_to_devnum <- function(x) x * 10 + mean(mmn_data$DevNum)   # back to 1-150 for the x-axis

as.data.frame(emm_dev) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = back_to_devnum(DevNum_gmc), y = emmean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = subject_lines, aes(x = back_to_devnum(x), y = MMN, group = SubjectID),
            color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = emmean - SE, ymax = emmean + SE), fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1.3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Deviant presentation number", y = "MMN (µV)",
       title = "The MMN habituates over the session",
       subtitle = "Orange = EMM ± 1 SE (average age); gray = each participant's model-estimated line")
```

```{r visualize-random-slopes-solution, fig.height=6, class.source = "fold-hide"}
# Each participant's random intercept and slope, + the fixed effects = their own MMN and habituation slope
subject_re_est <- as.data.frame(ranef(fit_final, condVar = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(grpvar == "SubjectID") %>%
  mutate(estimate = condval + fixef(fit_final)[as.character(term)],   # fixed effect + random effect
         lower    = estimate - 1.96 * condsd,                          # 95% interval of each participant's estimate
         upper    = estimate + 1.96 * condsd)

hab_slopes <- subject_re_est %>%
  filter(term == "DevNum_gmc") %>%
  mutate(SubjectID = fct_reorder(grp, estimate))                      # order participants by their slope

ggplot(hab_slopes, aes(x = estimate, y = SubjectID)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fixef(fit_final)[["DevNum_gmc"]], color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), height = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(color = "#3D6080", size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7)) +
  labs(x = "Habituation slope (change in MMN per 10 deviants, µV)", y = "Participant",
       title = "Each participant's habituation slope (the by-participant random slope)",
       subtitle = "Orange = fixed effect (average slope); dashed = no habituation; bars = 95% interval")
```

```{r visualize-random-slope-correlation-solution, fig.height=4.5, class.source = "fold-hide"}
subject_re_est %>%
  select(SubjectID = grp, term, estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = estimate) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `(Intercept)`, y = DevNum_gmc)) +
  geom_point(color = "#3D6080", size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Participant's MMN (middle of the session, µV)",
       y = "Participant's habituation slope (µV per 10 deviants)",
       title = "Participants' MMN vs. their habituation",
       subtitle = paste0("Each point = one participant; model correlation = ",
                         round(attr(VarCorr(fit_final)$SubjectID, "correlation")[1, 2], 2)))
```


# Additional ideas to explore

- **Fit Model B.** If you hypothesized that the habituation rate changes with
  age, fit the second maximal model from Step 5 (`DevNum_gmc * Age_gmc`) and
  simplify it with the same leave-one-out approach. Which term would you
  remove first? Do you end up at the same random-effects structure?
- **Change the simulation.** Go back to the design parameters, make the tokens
  differ more (`token_sd`) or simulate fewer participants, and rerun
  everything. Which simplification steps change?
- **Model the standards and deviants directly.** The supplement
  (`LME_ex2_supplement_interaction.Rmd`) fits the same pairs as a Condition ×
  Age interaction and compares the two approaches.
